results.title: The $500 Billion Buys the Factories. Utilization Decides the Winners.
highlights:
Launch a GPU on Jarvislabs — from $0.41/hr

H100s, H200s, A100s and more — per-second billing, no commitments.

...

Historically, compute was considered a depreciating asset. Nvidia ships a new GPU generation every two to three years, and the standing question was

...

Two years back, the market behaved exactly that way. A huge wave of supply came in, and providers competed by cutting prices on H100s and H200s. It looked like a race to the bottom.

Over the last year, we've watched that trend reverse. Prices are increasing. Availability has gone down. And customers who used to rent by the hour now want to commit for much longer durations, to make sure the compute they need for their workloads is actually there.

The numbers on our own platform tell the story. When I wrote this in August, our on-demand price was $2.69 per hour for an H100 and $3.99 for an H200, already 20 to 30% higher than a year earlier. As of October 5, it is $3.49 for an H100 and $4.59 for an H200, another 30% and 15% on top of that. For committed capacity, pricing depends on cluster size and duration: a large H200 cluster runs anywhere between $3.20 and $4.00 per hour, and a two- or three-year contract can bring that toward the lower end of $3 to $4.

Here's the detail that surprises people: when customers want an instant cluster, capacity right now rather than next quarter, they usually end up paying more than the on-demand price. Scarcity has inverted the old discount logic.

Nvidia cited the same trend in its announcement: one-year H100 rentals rose from about $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026, and cross-provider on-demand medians moved from roughly $2.00 to $2.70. We saw the same movement in our own pricing well before the announcement. The asset is holding value.

results.title: The H100 Is Three Years Old and Its Rent Just Went Up 60 Percent
highlights:
In January, a one-year contract on an H100 cleared at somewhere between $1.50 and $2.05 per GPU hour. In July, it cleared between $2.40 and $3.20. At the midpoint, that is a rise of roughly 58 percent in six months.

...

It should be getting cheaper. Owners should be preparing to write it down.

Instead, the on-demand market for H100 capacity has been sold out in five of the last six months. The tenants holding nodes are refusing to release them back into the pool, and are paying above $2.70 an hour to keep them.

...

The move was broad. Not one SKU in one market. Between January and July, contract pricing rose across every generation of accelerator being rented, including those meant to be on their way out.

Hopper led it. H100 one month rates moved from a $1.75 to $2.10 band to $2.90 to $3.30. H200 was stronger still: one year contracts went from roughly $2.03 at the midpoint to $3.45, an increase of about 70 percent. H200 on demand capacity has been sold out for six consecutive months, with existing tenants paying above $2.90 to hold what they have.

Blackwell moved in the same direction from a higher base. B200 three year contracts rose about 42 percent at the midpoint. B300 two year contracts rose about 39 percent. GB300 three year contracts went from roughly $3.58 to $5.00, and the five year from $3.10 to $4.60, a rise of 48 percent on the longest tenor quoted. B200, B300 and H200 on demand have each been marked sold out every month since February.

AMD, which is usually the release valve when Nvidia capacity is out of reach. This time it moved too. MI300 on-demand went from a $1.50 to $2.00 band in November to $2.50 to $2.70 in July. MI325 one-year contracts rose 63 percent over the same window. The substitution route is repricing as fast as the thing being substituted for. Of all, it is the strongest. That is a 48 percent increase in three months on hardware that is still ramping into volume shipment. A five-year commitment on Rubin now prices roughly 65 percent above a five-year commitment on GB300.

It is not a survey artefact. It is a clearing price.

results.title: AI Inference Token Costs Fall 37.5% as GPU Rental Fees Rise 15.2%, Power Crunch Extends Infrastructure Timeline to 5-10 Years | Gate News
highlights: According to Citi analyst Heath Terry's latest AI industry tracker, inference token costs have fallen 37.5% from May peaks to $1.33 per million tokens in Q2, while Blackwell GPU rental fees rose 15.2% to $5.18 per hour. This divergence reflects intelligent routing systems that automatically assign models by task complexity, lowering costs systematically. However, power constraints, licensing delays, and labor shortages have lengthened infrastructure production capacity expansion from an initial 3-year timeline to 5-10 years. Data centers now account for approximately 90% of new power grid applications.

results.title: The Coming NeoCloud Price War Is Just Beginning | Stephen Diamond
highlights: The Coming NeoCloud Price War Is Just Beginning The first generation of NeoCloud economics was remarkably simple: GPU × hours × price. Rent an H100, run your training job, pay the bill. That model made sense when AI infrastructure was dominated by training, but the massive shift toward inference is fundamentally changing how AI compute is priced. Consider current market dynamics. Published H100 pricing varies widely depending on provider, configuration, and purchasing model—ranging from Crusoe listing H100 HGX capacity at ~$3.90/GPU-hour down to RunPod advertising H100 PCIe capacity below $3.00/hour. More importantly, we are seeing a rapid proliferation of pricing structures. Markets are moving away from monolithic hourly rentals toward multi-tiered models including spot capacity, serverless scaling, and second-by-second metering (e.g., RunPod’s Flex vs. Active workers). This shift happens because training and inference operate on fundamentally different economics.. Training is a pure capacity problem: you need 1,000 tightly interconnected GPUs running at 90%+ utilization for 90 days. Inference, by contrast, is plagued by fluctuating demand, strict latency SLAs, and variable memory constraints. An idle $2.00/hour spot instance running at 30% utilization actually costs an effective $6.67/hour. Consequently, evaluating efficiency purely on nominal $/GPU-hour is obsolete. The operational benchmark is moving toward outcome-based pricing, where customers pay directly for completed, SLA-compliant tasks rather than underlying compute cycles. This price war will likely trigger three major structural shifts across the industry: 1. NeoCloud Consolidation: As raw GPU rental margins collapse by an estimated 30–50%, low-tier NeoClouds that rely solely on reselling raw hardware will be squeezed out or acquired. Only capital-efficient providers with proprietary software layers will survive. At the same time, lower-cost distributed compute models will begin to proliferate. 2. Emergence of Aggregation & Routing Layers: Enormous economic value will migrate upward to smart orchestration platforms—software layers that dynamically broker and route workloads across dozens of providers, spot markets, models and accelerator architectures in real time. 3 Vertical Integration and Specialized Inferencing: To avoid commodity price wars, some surviving NeoClouds will re-architect themselves into domain-specific stacks, bundling tailored hardware with specialized software for vertical workloads like drug discovery, real-time video rendering, or autonomous agent execution. The Bottom Line: The NeoCloud sector is about to transform from being a hardware rental business into an algorithmic marketplace for delivering intelligence. The winners won't be defined by who owns the most silicon, but by who controls the most sophisticated software layers capable of routing, optimizing, and pricing workloads anywhere, anytime on an outcome basis at the lowest possible cost.

results.title: [CoreWeave Q2 2026 Earnings Call] Revenue Soars 112% to $2.6 Billion as CoreWeave Raises Annual Guidance and Adds Record 500 MW Capacity
highlights:
CoreWeave delivered an exceptional second quarter of fiscal 2026, with revenue surging 112% year-over-year to a record $2.6 billion and adjusted operating income swinging from just $21 million in Q1 to $128 million, marking a clear inflection in operating leverage. The AI cloud provider added a record ~500 MW of active power, more than any prior quarter, and ended June with 1.5 GW live. Managed inference booked annual recurring revenue exploded from $1 million to over $100 million in a single quarter, with a year-end target of $250 million. The company also raised its full-year revenue guidance to $12.4–$ 13.2 billion, adjusted operating income to $960 million–$ 1.15 billion, and its exit annualized run-rate target to $18.5–$ 19.5 billion. CEO Mike Intrator pointed to intensifying demand across all GPU generations, with new contracts showing contribution margins 5–10 percentage points higher than recent quarters and a 25% price increase implemented in July. The backlog grew 246% year-over-year to $104 billion, and an additional $25 billion in net new commitments were signed early in Q3. With contracted power reaching 4.2 GW and international expansion underway, CoreWeave sees demand exceeding supply for years.

...

Pricing is the other engine. A 25% increase across all SKUs was implemented in July, but even before that, margins on new contracts were already 5 to 10 percentage points higher than in recent quarters. Intrator attributed the margin expansion to customers’ growing realization that CoreWeave’s platform delivers superior total cost of ownership and application performance, as well as the fact that many clients are now monetizing their AI products and are willing to pay a premium for scarce compute.

results.title: Google Cloud's flexible commitments now discount G2 and G4 GPU VMs
highlights:
Since August 11, 2026, spend-based flexible CUDs cover G4 (RTX PRO 6000) VMs at 16% off for 1 year or 42% for 3 years, and G2 (L4) at 21% or 43%, with no GPU reservation needed.

By Saurabh Khatri · Published Oct 18, 2026

Google Cloud made its compute flexible committed use discounts (CUDs) generally available for the G2 and G4 GPU machine series on August 11, 2026. G2 VMs use NVIDIA L4 GPUs and G4 VMs use NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. A flexible CUD is a commitment to an hourly spend rather than to specific machines, and the release note says that for these GPUs it needs no attached reservation.

## The discounts

Google’s committed use discounts overview lists these rates for flexible CUDs:

| What is covered | 1-year term | 3-year term |
| --- | --- | --- |
| G2: vCPUs, memory and NVIDIA L4 GPUs | 21% | 43% |
| G4: vCPUs, memory and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs | 16% | 42% |
| Most general-purpose series, for comparison | 28% | 46% |

GPUs are covered only on G2 and G4. No other accelerator-optimized machine series is on the list of eligible series, so this doesn’t apply to Google’s other GPU machine types.

## How a flexible commitment works

- You commit to a minimum hourly spend on eligible resources, not to a number of GPUs.
- You pay that hourly amount for the whole term, whether or not you use it.
- The commitment applies to eligible spend across Compute Engine, GKE and Cloud Run.
- You can switch between eligible machine series and regions and keep the discount.
- Local SSD disks on these series are covered too.

A commitment bought in the first 49 minutes of an hour starts at the next hour; one bought later starts the hour after that.

...

Commit only to the hourly spend you are sure to use for the full term, because unused commitment is still billed. On G4 the 1-year discount is small at 16%, so weigh it against the 42% 3-year rate and how long you expect to need the GPUs.

So, which GPU cloud provider is best for AI, and how much should you expect to pay?

...

Current comparisons show CoreWeave can be competitive with hyperscalers for specialized AI workloads, particularly when customers use reserved capacity. One April 2026 analysis reported CoreWeave reserved B200 pricing starting around $2.65 per GPU/hour for annual commitments.

...

Spot pricing can also make Google Cloud significantly more competitive for workloads that can tolerate interruptions. A July 2026 pricing tracker reported H100 spot pricing around $2.25 per GPU/hour, although rates vary by region and availability.

...

# How Much Does GPU Cloud Hosting Cost?

GPU pricing can range from a few cents per hour for lower-end or marketplace hardware to more than $10 per hour for powerful enterprise GPUs and configurations.

Current 2026 GPU price trackers show enormous variation across providers and hardware types. One live comparison lists hundreds of GPU configurations across dozens of providers, with prices ranging from fractions of a dollar per hour to well above $10 per hour.

For high-end AI GPUs, approximate market ranges can look like this:

| GPU | Approximate cloud range |
| --- | --- |
| RTX 4090 | ~$0.30–$1.00/hr |
| A100 | ~$1.00–$3.50/hr |
| H100 | ~$2.00–$7.00+/hr |
| H200 | ~$3.00–$8.00+/hr |
| B200 | ~$3.50–$14.00+/hr |

These are indicative 2026 ranges, not universal prices. The actual price depends on provider, region, memory configuration, reservation, spot/on-demand status and availability. Current comparisons show, for example, B200 pricing ranging from approximately $3.49/hour at Lambda to around $14.24/hour for certain AWS configurations.

...

# On-Demand vs Spot vs Reserved GPU Hosting

The billing model can have an enormous impact on your costs.

## On-Demand

You pay the standard hourly rate.

Best for:

- Production inference
- Development
- Unpredictable workloads
- Applications that require immediate availability

## Spot

You use spare capacity at a discounted price.

Best for:

- Training
- Batch jobs
- Experiments
- Fault-tolerant workloads

The downside is that the instance may be interrupted.

Google Cloud spot pricing, for example, can reduce H100 costs substantially compared with on-demand rates.

## Reserved/Committed

You commit to using infrastructure for a longer period.

Best for:

- Constant inference
- Long-term training
- Production workloads
- Predictable demand

The provider gives you a lower effective hourly price in exchange for the commitment.

results.title: OVH Cloud warns of 87% price hikes to help it cover RAMpocalypse costs
highlights:
Octave Klaba, the CEO of France-based cloud operator OVH, has warned that it will soon hike the price of server rental by up to 87 percent.

Klaba said the price OVH pays for memory rose 6x in the year to June 2026, will rise to 9x by September, and hit 12x next year. He has also seen a 7x price increase for NVMe drives, hard disk prices rise 3.5x, and the cost of CPUs, motherboards, and network cards rise by 15 to 20 percent. He thinks those prices will climb further in the near future, and blames the hyperscale buying frenzy sparked by the AI boom for the increases.

Writing on X, Klaba said OVH recently received quotes for RAM and disk prices, and argued the company must pass on its increased costs by hiking the prices for new servers as it brings them online.

The biggest rise will come to those who rent 2026-edition gaming servers, whose bills will jump by 87 percent. The cost of other recent servers will increase by 40 to 59 percent. The increases kick in from September.

The Euro-cloud will also increase the price it charges to access its 2024-era equipment when customers renew contracts, but by less than the increase charged to use new machines.

“A customer already equipped will therefore see an increase 3 to 6 times lower than for a new order,” reads a machine translation of Klaba’s Xeets.

The company is also changing the way it charges for some services, for example by decoupling storage and IP addresses from its Gen3 instances, to become separately billed line items from October 1 st. OVH will charge €0.000146/GB/h for storage, and €0.0027/h for IP.

Another change will see the company drop its one-month, six-month, and 24-month saving plans that lock in prices for the duration of a contract. 12 and 36 month saving plans remain.

...

“We don't know the price level of RAM and drives in 2027 yet, but the probability that prices will continue to rise is very high,” he added, before teasing us all with the prospect of eventual relief.
